title: Six Important Findings from the AI in Action Learning Tour
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer, who builds tools for teachers at Amplify, argues that the AI in Action Learning Tour from Emily Freitag and Instruction Partners is the ethnographic study of AI in classrooms that funders should have commissioned four years ago. Instead of efficacy benchmarks, the tour watched real classrooms and real products. Meyer pulls out six findings: bet on teachers by building tools with a clear view of the teacher's role, decide whether you are working with or against the core curriculum, give teachers actionable next steps they can override, treat multilingual translation as a promising use, accept that many AI tools are dreary and no better than paper, and recognize that Google Search's AI Overview may be the hardest AI to ban. The post closes with commentary on a survivorship-biased AI tutoring study and on public opinion shifting toward schools that prohibit AI. Meyer's through-line is that how students and teachers actually use a tool matters more than whether it works in a controlled study.
points: Funders poured money into efficacy studies before anyone understood how students and teachers actually interact with generative AI, so the field is only now getting the observational evidence it needed.
Teacher-facing tools get used consistently only when they hold a clear point of view on what a teacher is supposed to do, and teachers prefer next-step suggestions they can modify or override.
Tools that sync tightly with a school's core curriculum are valued, so a product must decide early whether it is amplifying or fighting that organizing force.
Observers saw many AI tools that were as dreary as, or worse than, paper-and-pencil practice, which means careful design and implementation are the real value drivers.
School AI bans may miss the largest risk, since students routinely copy Google's AI Overview without reading it.
quotes: Four years ago, all of the big foundations and funders correctly identified generative AI as a Pretty Big Deal in education, a powerful new technology arriving at the classroom door without any warning.
Those funders seemed much more eager to answer the question “does this work when students use it?” than “how do students use it?” or even “do students want to use it?
Products with a clearer perspective on the teacher’s role were used more in line with their intended approach and more consistently across classrooms.
Teachers valued insights that they could act on while the lesson was still live and nudges that prompted them to support individual learners’ needs rather than only class averages.

Some products let students respond in their home language and give the teacher an English version to read, so a teacher who doesn’t speak the student’s language can still follow the thinking and respond to it.
We saw students go through the motions of learning without internalizing much—experiences that were isolating and boring to students.
But I did regularly see students open their search browser, ask a question, and copy the “AI Overview” summary without questioning it or—as far as I could tell—usually even reading it.
